description: Jaguar Code is a team of two developers from Cochabamba, Bolivia. Jose Luis Larrazabal (CTO) leads the architecture, reviews every change and deploys the web app and the APK. Pedro Rolon Fenalti works on the NASA data, the validation against the SMAP satellite and the pitch. We built CHAKRA with AI coding assistants, and every change passes tests and human review before it is merged.
summary:
CHAKRA, named after the Quechua word for a farm plot, helps smallholder farmers in the valleys of Cochabamba, Bolivia, compare crop rotations before planting. It compares the farmer’s current rotation with two alternatives, showing water shortfall, frost risk, and months without crop cover.

The project addresses “Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data” by translating 25 years of daily NASA POWER climate data into understandable agricultural comparisons using the FAO-56 method. It covers La Maica, Distrito 9, and Distrito 13. The model was checked against 150 weeks of NASA SMAP soil-moisture observations, with agreement in approximately seven out of ten weekly dry, normal, or wet categories.

CHAKRA is accessible through a web application and an Android APK. It communicates its limitations: regional data does not describe individual plots, irrigation is excluded, and no agronomist has reviewed the results. CHAKRA supports informed decisions while leaving the final choice to the farmer.
details:
CHAKRA is a crop-rotation comparison tool developed by Jaguar Code for smallholder farmers in the valleys of Cochabamba, Bolivia. Its name comes from the Quechua word for a farm plot. The project makes NASA Earth observation and climate data understandable before a farmer commits to a planting decision.

Users select La Maica, Distrito 9, or Distrito 13 and compare three rotations: maize followed by bare soil, maize followed by broad bean, and potato followed by pea. Each comparison presents estimated water shortfall under historically dry, normal, and wet conditions, frost risk, and months without crop cover. A monthly calendar helps users understand when these trade-offs occur.

The Python engine processes daily NASA POWER temperature, precipitation, humidity, wind, and solar-radiation data. Historical rotation comparisons use the 2001–2025 record, while recent conditions incorporate available 2026 observations. Reference evapotranspiration is calculated using the FAO-56 Penman–Monteith equation, followed by a daily root-zone soil-water balance. Crop coefficients, rooting depths, and soil-water assumptions are documented using FAO references. NASA SRTM elevation data supports a temperature adjustment for each zone.

The model’s weekly soil-moisture behavior was compared with NASA SMAP observations over 150 weeks, from July 2022 through June 2025. Approximately seven out of ten weeks fell into the same dry, normal, or wet category. This is agreement between categories, not a claim of 70% forecasting accuracy. SMAP observes the near-surface soil, while the model represents the root zone; the comparison therefore has important limitations.

CHAKRA includes Chakarero, an experimental AI assistant that receives the application’s data as context to answer questions. It uses the open-weight model openai/gpt-oss-120b through Groq. The assistant is separate from the numerical agricultural model, and its responses can be incorrect.

The application is designed for mobile use, with readable text, strong contrast, and risk communicated through words and visual indicators. The app supports Spanish and English, with a partial Quechua translation pending linguistic validation. The landing page includes Spanish, English, and a preliminary Quechua translation. An Android application packages the web experience using Expo and React Native WebView.

The prototype has explicit limits. Its data represents zones rather than individual plots. The three zones share a NASA POWER grid cell. Irrigation is excluded, soil properties are assumed rather than measured locally, and no agronomist has reviewed the numerical results. Demonstration plots must not be mistaken for monitored farms. CHAKRA supports the farmer’s decision rather than replacing local knowledge or professional advice.

The intended impact is to make the consequences of crop-rotation choices easier to understand before planting. Future plans include collecting farmers’ records with consent, moving from historical comparisons toward prediction, and developing municipal data marts. These remain future work.

Development used Python, TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Expo, React Native WebView, and Vercel. AI assistants supported coding, debugging, research, writing, translation, visual design, and presentation preparation. Chakarero’s supplied pixel-art illustration is AI-generated. Agricultural calculations come from the documented numerical engine and cited data sources.

The team is Jaguar Code: Pedro Rolon Fenalti and Jose Luis Larrazabal.
